title: Deadly Intel Fab 28 Explosion Threatens $600 Million in Revenue as Server Supply Tightens
author: Daniel Nenni
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

An explosion at Intel’s Fab 28 manufacturing facility in Kiryat Gat, Israel, killed two workers, seriously injured another and forced a shutdown lasting approximately two weeks. Intel now estimates the disruption will reduce revenue by roughly $600 million across two quarters, adding pressure to an already constrained server processor business.

During Intel’s October 29 earnings call, Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner estimated a $300 million revenue impact in the fourth quarter of 2026, with a similar reduction expected in the first quarter of 2027. Almost all the fourth-quarter shortfall involves server products manufactured using Intel’s 10nm-class technology, according to management.

Intel expected production to begin restarting by the end of the week. However, restarting equipment does not immediately restore shipments. The company is examining wafers that were undergoing fabrication when operations stopped, determining which remain usable. Most associated wafer write-offs are expected during the fourth quarter, concentrating the immediate margin damage.

The distinction between shutdown duration and commercial impact matters. Intel described approximately two weeks without production and shipment effects spanning two quarters. It has not confirmed six continuous months of severe manufacturing disruption, disclosed when full capacity will return, or identified precisely which Xeon processor families face the greatest supply reductions.

The accident compounds existing bottlenecks. Management identified Intel 3 manufacturing constraints and shortages of advanced packaging substrates alongside the Israeli outage. Demand for data center products already exceeds available supply, meaning the loss of otherwise productive capacity makes it harder to translate strong customer orders into near-term revenue and delivered systems.

For server customers, the practical concern is procurement uncertainty during expanding AI infrastructure investment. Reduced processor availability could complicate deployment schedules and allocations. The financial estimate remains preliminary, and Intel has cautioned that wafer assessments could change its understanding of the damage. Further recovery disclosures will determine the eventual operational impact.
